articles.title: The Prayer List That Included Nero
articles.dek: Paul told a frightened young pastor to pray for the most dangerous man in the empire. What was he thinking?
articles.quote: You don't have to agree with a leader to pray for them. You only have to believe God is bigger than the throne they sit on.
articles.body:
On the night of February 22, 1986, a line of Marcos-loyalist tanks rolled down Ortigas Avenue toward a crowd of unarmed Filipinos. There was nothing between the tanks and the people except a handful of nuns from the Daughters of St. Paul. They did not run. They knelt in the street, rosaries in their hands, and began praying out loud — for the soldiers inside those tanks, for the generals who sent them, even for the president whose government had jailed priests and silenced newspapers for fourteen years. Within hours, soldiers were climbing out of their vehicles to accept flowers and rosary beads from the very people they had been ordered to disperse. Not a single shot was fired that night. Historians still call it one of the most peaceful revolutions in modern history, and it started with women on their knees, praying for the men who held the guns.

That image is worth holding onto as you read one of the more surprising verses in all of Paul's letters. Timothy was a young pastor, probably in his thirties, trying to hold together a fragile church in Ephesus. Paul, likely nearing the end of his life, writes to coach him through it. And the very first instruction Paul gives — before anything about church structure, before anything about elders or deacons — is about prayer. Not prayer in general. Prayer for a very specific category of person.

"I urge, then, first of all," Paul writes, "that petitions, prayers, intercession and thanksgiving be made for all people — for kings and all those in authority" (1 Timothy 2:1-2). Read that again slowly. Paul doesn't say pray for good kings, or kings who treat the church fairly, or kings who share your values. He says pray for kings. Full stop. And when Paul wrote those words, sometime in the mid-60s AD, the king on the throne was Nero.

Nero was not a minor inconvenience. By the time this letter was written, he had already arranged the murder of his own mother. He would soon blame Christians for the Great Fire of Rome and have them tortured in his gardens as entertainment. This was not an abstract "authority" Paul had in mind. This was the single most dangerous man in the known world to the very people Paul was writing to. And Paul's instruction to Timothy's congregation was: put him on your prayer list. First of all.

"I urge, then, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercession and thanksgiving be made for all people — for kings and all those in authority, that we may live peaceful and quiet lives in all godliness and holiness." (1 Timothy 2:1-2, NIV)

Here's what's easy to miss on a first read: Paul doesn't ground this instruction in Nero's character. He grounds it in God's character. Look at what follows just two verses later — this kind of prayer "is good, and pleases God our Savior, who wants all people to be saved and to come to a knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:3-4). The reason to pray for a hostile ruler isn't that he deserves it. It's that God hasn't given up on him, and neither should the church. Prayer for the throne is an act of hope, not approval.

It's worth asking why Paul places this instruction first, ahead of everything else he's about to say about how the church should order its life together. Maybe it's because a church that has stopped praying for the people in power has quietly started trusting those people more than it trusts God — either fearing them too much, or resenting them too much, or simply assuming prayer won't change anything that matters. Paul interrupts all of that in a single sentence. Before Timothy organizes anything else, Paul wants him to make sure the church hasn't let fear or contempt crowd out intercession.

This is where the nuns on Ortigas Avenue become more than a nice story. They had every reason to distrust the government bearing down on them. Years of martial law had given them a long list of grievances. And yet their first move, facing down tanks, was not a chant or a shout. It was a prayer — for the very men sent to clear them off the road. That is not naivety. That is the same conviction Paul hands to Timothy: that the people who frighten you most are still within reach of God's mercy, and your prayer might be part of how that mercy arrives.

Think about who sits on your own list of hard names. Maybe it's a national leader whose decisions you can't stand. Maybe it's smaller and closer — a boss, a landlord, a barangay official who never returns your calls, a relative with more power in the family than wisdom. Paul's instruction doesn't ask you to approve of them. It asks you to pray for them, by name, as a first priority rather than an afterthought squeezed in after you've prayed for everyone easier to love.

Try this tonight. Write down one name — someone in authority over some part of your life whom you find difficult to pray for. Then actually pray for them: not that they would simply get out of your way, but that they would come, as Paul puts it, "to a knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4). You may not see Nero turn into a different man. The nuns on Ortigas Avenue didn't get to choose the outcome of that night either. But they knelt anyway, and history still remembers what happened when they did. Your prayer for one difficult name on your list may not rewrite a nation. It might just loosen something quieter and nearer: the grip that name has had on your own heart.

articles.title: The Basket They Called Good
articles.dek: A prophet is shown two baskets of figs outside a ransacked temple — and told, to everyone's shock, which one is the lucky one.
articles.quote: God didn't call the exiles good because of where they ended up. He called them good because of what he intended to do in them there.
articles.body:
In February 1945, a young Soviet artillery officer named Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was pulled off the front lines and arrested. His crime was a letter to a friend, mildly mocking Stalin. For that, he lost eight years to the Gulag — frozen labor camps, starvation rations, a body worked past what it could give. On paper, nothing worse could have happened to him. Meanwhile, the officers who stayed behind kept their medals, their apartments, their comfortable places inside a system built on lies.

Years later, Solzhenitsyn wrote something that stunned his readers. Of the camp that broke his health and stole a decade of his life, he said: "Bless you, prison, for having been in my life." It was in the Gulag, not before it, that his faith returned, his writing found its purpose, and his soul — his word — grew strong enough to outlast the empire that imprisoned him. The men who avoided his fate, who kept their comfortable posts, mostly stayed exactly as small as the system needed them to be.

Centuries earlier, a prophet in a ruined city saw the same strange math play out — and God himself was the one doing the sorting.

It's 597 BC. Babylon's army has just dragged King Jeconiah, the royal family, and Jerusalem's skilled craftsmen and leading citizens off into exile. The ones left behind are, understandably, relieved. They kept their houses. They kept the temple. They kept a king on the throne — Zedekiah, installed by Babylon as a placeholder. By every visible measure, staying was the better outcome. Leaving in chains was the curse.

Then the Lord shows Jeremiah a vision, set deliberately in front of the temple. Two baskets of figs. One basket holds figs "like those that ripen early" — plump, sweet, the best of the crop. The other holds figs "so bad they cannot be eaten." Jeremiah doesn't have to guess which is which; the Lord tells him outright. The good figs are the exiles — the very people everyone assumed God had abandoned to Babylon. The rotten figs are Zedekiah, his officials, and everyone left comfortably in Jerusalem.

Read what God says about the basket nobody wanted to be in:

"Like these good figs, I regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I sent away from this place to the land of the Babylonians. My eyes will watch over them for their good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not uproot them. I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the Lord. They will be my people, and I will be their God, for they will return to me with all their heart." (Jeremiah 24:5–7, NIV)

Notice what God does not say. He doesn't say the exile will be painless. He doesn't say it will be short. He says, in effect: this is where I'm going to do my deepest work in you. The chains, the long walk to a foreign land, the loss of home and temple and status — none of that disqualifies them from God's good purpose. It's the very setting for it. I will give them a heart to know me — that line is almost shocking. God is promising that the hardship itself will produce something the comfortable life back home never managed to: a heart that actually knows him.

Meanwhile the figs left in the basket of "safety" are the ones God calls ruined beyond saving (Jeremiah 24:8–10). Not because exile is virtuous and comfort is sinful — that's not the point. It's that comfort had let Zedekiah's Jerusalem drift so far from God that judgment, not blessing, was what remained for them there. The place that looked safest was, underneath, the more dangerous place to be.

It's worth sitting with how backwards this feels. We size up our situations by what we can see: who kept their job, whose family stayed together, who got to remain in the place they loved. We assume God's favor tracks with comfort and his absence tracks with loss. Jeremiah's vision quietly overturns that math. Good figs and bad figs were never about which basket looked better at the market. They were about where God intended to do his work.

Maybe you know this from the inside. Maybe an OFW reading this is three time zones from home tonight, missing a child's birthday for the fourth year running, wondering if being far away means being forgotten. Maybe you're the one who got let go while your officemates kept their desks, or the one whose marriage ended while your friends' anniversaries kept rolling by. The temptation is to read your basket as proof of God's verdict on you. Jeremiah 24 says: not so fast. The exiles didn't do anything to earn the good basket. They were simply the ones God chose to watch over, build up, and give a new heart — right there in Babylon, long before the forty years of distance ever ended.

This doesn't mean every hard season is secretly a blessing in disguise, or that we should go looking for exile. Solzhenitsyn never asked for the Gulag, and Jeremiah never pretended Babylon was a vacation. But both stories insist that God is not limited by geography. He doesn't need you home to be good to you. He doesn't need your circumstances to look fortunate before he starts building, planting, and giving you a heart that knows him.

So if you're in a season that feels like the bad basket — uprooted, far from where you wanted to be, surrounded by people who seem to have it easier — ask a different question than why me. Ask what Jeremiah's exiles eventually learned to ask: what is God doing in me, here, that he might not have done anywhere else? Keep that question somewhere you'll see it this week. The answer may take longer than you'd like. But God already told Jeremiah how the story ends for the basket that looked lost: watched over, built up, planted, and given a heart that finally knows him. That's not a bad basket to be in after all.

articles.title: Water Out of Stone
articles.dek: A Roman engineer once had to climb back into an unfinished mountain tunnel to find where two crews digging blind in the dark had missed each other. Psalm 114 says that is exactly the kind of hidden, hard place where God turns rock into water.
articles.quote: The same hand that turned the sea to dry ground can turn your hardest place into a spring.
articles.body:
In the hills of Roman North Africa, sometime in the second century AD, two teams of diggers broke ground on opposite sides of the same mountain. Their job was to carve a tunnel straight through solid rock near Saldae, the town we now call Bejaia, in Algeria, so a spring on the far side could finally reach the thirsty town below. Each crew worked by torchlight, swinging picks into stone they could not see past, trusting a surveyor's calculations that somewhere in the dark heart of that mountain, their two tunnels would meet. There was no sound down there but iron on rock and the slow, patient breathing of men who had no proof yet that the work was going anywhere at all.

They did not meet. An ancient inscription that survives to this day tells us why. The engineer who had planned the project, a Roman surveyor named Nonius Datus, had moved on to other assignments by the time digging began. Left without him, the two crews drifted off course underground, each tunnel growing longer and longer, passing the other in the dark without ever touching. Years of labor, and the mountain still held its water hostage. Town officials, afraid the whole costly project was lost, sent an urgent summons for Nonius Datus to come back. He made the difficult journey, climbed down into the unfinished tunnels himself, found exactly where the lines had drifted apart, and ordered new connecting passages dug to join them. After more months of blind chiseling, pickaxes finally broke through into open air on the far side. Water ran the whole length of the mountain, and in Nonius Datus's own words, carved into stone, the town received its water "to the joy of all."

Centuries before that tunnel was ever dug, an Israelite poet wrote a psalm about a very different rock giving up its water, not through careful engineering, but through the bare presence of God. Psalm 114 opens quietly with Israel's exit from Egypt: "Judah became God's sanctuary, Israel his dominion" (v.2), a people who had been slaves becoming, almost overnight, the very place where God chose to dwell. Then the psalm gets strange, in the best way. The sea looked at what was happening and fled, the way the Red Sea once stood back to let a frightened nation walk through on dry ground. The Jordan River turned around and ran backward, the way it would later pile up so the same people could cross into a new land. "The mountains leaped like rams, the hills like lambs" (v.4), the whole landscape caught up in something that sounds less like an earthquake and more like a flock let loose into spring pasture at the sound of a familiar voice.

Then the poet does something unexpected. He turns and interrogates the very things he just described, as if creation owes him an explanation. "Why was it, sea, that you fled? Why, Jordan, did you turn back? Why, mountains, did you leap like rams, you hills, like lambs?" (vv.5-6). It reads almost like a parent crouching down to ask a child why they suddenly bolted across the yard, gently, not angrily, just wanting to understand. And instead of answering his own question, the poet simply names who had arrived.

"Tremble, earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob, who turned the rock into a pool of water, the hard rock into springs of water." (Psalm 114:7-8, NIV)

It helps to sit with that word tremble for a moment, because it is easy to misread as terror. The Hebrew picture behind it is closer to a held breath than to fear of punishment, the kind of trembling a person feels standing very close to something enormous and holy, like the hush that falls over a room at the sound of a newborn's first cry. The earth does not shake here because God is dangerous. It shakes because he is near, and nearness to him is its own kind of overwhelming.

Notice what the psalm does not do, though. It never actually explains why the sea fled or why the mountains skipped like young rams let out to open ground. It simply names who showed up. That, apparently, was reason enough. The sea did not need a committee meeting to decide whether God's presence mattered. It fled on sight, instantly, completely, without a moment of arguing. It is worth sitting quietly with what it would look like for us to recognize his nearness that fast, needing no further explanation than that he is close.

There is something else easy to miss in verse 8. "The rock into a pool of water, the hard rock into springs of water" is a quiet callback to two desert crises recorded in Exodus 17 and Numbers 20, at a place called Rephidim and later Meribah, when Israel ran out of water in the wilderness and turned on Moses in near-rebellion. Moses struck flint-hard rock with a shepherd's staff, and water came pouring out in front of the whole camp. Those were not gentle chapters. They were full of grumbling, threats, even Moses's own temper getting the better of him. But the psalm does not mention any of that. Looking back across the centuries, the poet chooses to remember only the water, not the complaining that provoked it. That is a kind of memory worth practicing on our own hard days, letting the miracle outshine the grumbling that came before it.

Most of us are not standing at a parted sea this week. More likely, we are somewhere in the middle of a tunnel, chiseling forward through something hard and dark, with no proof yet that the other side exists. A marriage that feels like solid rock. A diagnosis that will not move. A financial wall that will not give an inch. A grief that has not softened in months of quiet nights and emptier mornings. Psalm 114 does not explain why the rock is hard, and it does not promise to tell us exactly when it will break open. What it offers instead is quieter, and in the end sturdier: the reminder of who is present in the tunnel with us, even while the two sides of our digging have not yet met. The same hand that turned the sea to dry ground can turn your hardest place into a spring.

Nonius Datus never saw his tunnel finished on the day he first surveyed it. He had to be called back into the middle of the mess, climb down into the dark a second time, and keep correcting the line until both sides finally touched. Maybe that is the posture worth holding onto tonight: not demanding to know why the rock has not given way yet, but quietly tracing, in prayer, exactly where God's presence meets you in the dark, and trusting that somewhere just ahead of your picks, the water is already on its way to meet you too.

articles.title: The Bird That Only Comes for the Wound
articles.dek: A small African bird exposed a myth about friendship that biologists believed for decades — and Solomon diagnosed the exact same pattern in people three thousand years earlier.
articles.quote: Wealth buys company, but it cannot buy character, and character is the only thing that survives when the money and the crowd are gone.
articles.body:
For most of the twentieth century, biologists held up one bird as nature's picture of a perfect friendship. The oxpecker, a small reddish-billed bird found across the savannas of Africa, spends its days riding on the backs of rhinos, buffalo, and giraffes, picking ticks off their hides. Textbooks called it a textbook case of mutualism. The host gets free pest control, the bird gets an easy meal, everybody wins. Tour guides still tell the story that way.

Then researchers started watching more closely, and the tidy story got complicated. Field studies found that oxpeckers don't only pick off parasites. They peck directly into open wounds and keep them raw so they can drink the blood underneath. Several studies found the birds favor hosts who are already wounded or heavily infested, because more sores mean more food, and when a host heals up or a more wounded animal wanders by, the oxpecker doesn't hesitate. It moves on. The relationship was never really about the rhino. It was about what the rhino had to offer.

Three thousand years ago, a wiser man than any biologist had already noticed the same pattern in people.

Solomon's proverbs were written, in large part, as survival wisdom for a royal court, a place thick with flatterers, hangers-on, and fortune seekers who knew exactly which backs to ride. By the time we reach chapter 19, he has already filled eighteen chapters with warnings about wise speech and the kind of friend worth keeping. Here, in just five short verses, he lays out a string of hard, clear-eyed observations about human nature: integrity outlasts cleverness, haste outruns wisdom, self-made trouble gets blamed on God, money buys company, and lies eventually catch up with the liar. It reads like a man who watched a thousand courtiers come and go, and learned to tell the difference between the ones who stayed for him and the ones who stayed for his table.

One line in particular cuts through all the others.

Wealth attracts many friends, but even the poor man's friend deserts him. (Proverbs 19:4)

Read that slowly. Solomon isn't being cynical for sport. He's describing something he actually watched happen: people circling a man's table while the food is good, and vanishing the moment the table goes bare. The company was real enough, in its way, but it was never actually friendship. It was oxpecker behavior. It fed on what the man had, not on who the man was.

What makes the proverb sting is the second half of the sentence. Solomon doesn't just say the rich man has many friends and the poor man has none. He says even the poor man's own friend, someone who presumably chose him, sat with him, knew him, deserts him once the resources run dry. The desertion isn't a stranger's. It's someone closer than that. That's the part that's hard to read without wincing, because most of us have stood on one side of that sentence or the other at some point.

It's worth asking, gently: which side have I been on? Have I been drawn to someone mostly for what being near them gets me, their connections, their generosity, the shine of being associated with their success? And on the harder days, when a friend's wounds were open and unflattering and inconvenient, did I lean in, or did I quietly drift toward someone less complicated?

Solomon isn't writing this to make us suspicious of everyone around us. He's writing it so we stop building our sense of worth on the wrong foundation. Notice how he opens this very section, one verse earlier than the famous line about wealth:

Better the poor whose walk is blameless than a fool whose lips are perverse. (Proverbs 19:1)

Put the two verses side by side and the contrast sharpens. Wealth buys company, but it cannot buy character, and character is the only thing that survives when the money and the crowd are gone. A blameless walk, plain and unglamorous, outlasts every fair-weather friendship it will ever stand next to. That's not a consolation prize for people who can't draw a crowd. It's the one asset that never migrates when the feeding gets better somewhere else.

And here is where something larger than good advice quietly steps into this passage. The pattern Solomon describes, love that follows resources, attention that follows advantage, is exactly the pattern the gospel breaks. Christ didn't come looking for a profitable relationship with the healthy and well-resourced. He was drawn to the very thing every oxpecker friendship eventually abandons: a person with nothing left to offer. And having found that person, he didn't peck the wound open to feed on it. He stayed to close it.

That is the opposite of every transaction Solomon warns us about in this chapter. It's a friendship that runs toward poverty instead of away from it, that shows up after the money is gone and the crowd has thinned and there is finally nothing left to attract anyone, and stays anyway.

So here is something practical to carry out of these five short verses. Think of one person in your life right now who is in a poor season, not necessarily financially, but relationally, emotionally, in health, in reputation. Someone whose table has gone bare. Then do the one thing an oxpecker never does. Stay without feeding on it. Call them. Sit with them. Don't require them to be interesting, resourced, or useful to you before you show up at their door.

And if you're the one in the bare season yourself, here is the comfort tucked inside this old, clear-eyed proverb. Your worth was never actually measured by who stayed. Solomon already told you where to put your weight, on a blameless walk, not on a crowded table. And the gospel tells you something even steadier than that. There is a Friend who was drawn to you not for what you had, but for what you needed, and he has never once, since the day he found you, gone looking for a better offer.
